title: After quiet days, NOAA SWPC next-day solar proton (S1) probabilities were 2.8 times too high in 2020-2026, mainly because forecasts stayed flat over 3 days while S1 events persist
abstract: We verified 11,238 daily SWPC proton (S1) probabilities from 1996 to 2026 against a GOES 5-minute >10 MeV series that we built and checked against SWPC reports. We pre-registered the hypotheses. In a forward test of Cycle 25 (2020-2026), day-1 forecasts of 40% or less gave 0.41 times the expected S1 days (95% interval 0.29-0.54), as in Cycle 24. The excess came from days with no S1 time at issue: 43 S1 days occurred against 121.5 expected (0.35, 0.26-0.47). Their skill against climatology fell from +0.30 (Cycle 23) to -0.05 (Cycle 25). Day-1 forecasts during events were calibrated (1.08). In an exploratory analysis, 88-95% of quiet-start forecasts give the same value for days 1, 2 and 3, but the observed S1-day frequency doubles from day 1 to day 3 because S1 events last more than one day. The resulting day-1 factor was 0.40-0.47 in all three cycles, and S1 episode durations predict 0.44-0.48. A pre-registered recalibration fitted on 2000-2019 lowered the 2020-2026 day-1 Brier score by 22% but did not help days 2-3. A lead-only correction lowered the quiet-start day-1 score by 17%. We found no change in S1 frequency per issued X-flare probability. Limitations: the GOES-R integral is rebuilt (93% S1-side agreement with SWPC reports), there are few Cycle 25 events, and the lead analysis was not pre-registered.

display.caption: After quiet days, SWPC issues nearly flat 3-day S1 probabilities (dashed), but the observed S1-day frequency (solid) rises with lead. Observed/expected and the lead factor, with 27-day block bootstrap 95% intervals, for Cycles 23-25. Short dashes give the lead factor predicted from S1 episode durations only.

Day-1 reliability of SWPC S1 probabilities by issue state (Wilson 95% intervals). After quiet days, forecasts of 5-40% are too high in all cycles and most in Cycle 25. After days with S1 time, forecasts are calibrated.
Truth checks: GOES maxima against SWPC-reported RSGA peaks (2013-2026), and annual S1 days against SWPC verification tables (2000-2013).
